text: In Qiskit, a qubit is really just an index into a QuantumRegister sitting inside a circuit object — you never have a qubit, you have a circuit and refer to its wires by position. Q# takes a different stance: a qubit is a real, first-class value in the language, requested from the runtime, held by a variable, and released when you're done with it.

Four things to get comfortable with: Qubit is an opaque type — no readable classical state, a handle rather than a container you can peek inside. use statements request qubits from the runtime, replacing the older using block form from earlier QDK versions. Qubit bracket n allocates a whole array at once, indexable like any array. And every qubit follows a scoped-lifetime model, automatically released at the end of its block.

Here's the pattern you already know from Chapter 1, named properly now: use allocates one qubit, starting in |0>. H puts it in superposition. M measures it, consuming that superposition and returning the classical result. use is the current syntax — it scopes the qubit to the enclosing block automatically, with no extra braces needed the way the old using block form required.

Most real algorithms need more than one qubit, so Q# lets you allocate a whole array at once. Here, qs is three qubits, each starting in |0>, indexed exactly like any array — qs of zero, qs of one, and so on. Each element is its own independent Qubit handle; the array is just a convenient way to manage many of them together instead of writing three separate use statements.

A qubit allocated with use is automatically released when control leaves its block — you never call a Release function yourself. But release carries an obligation: on simulators that track exact state, releasing a qubit still in an unknown superposition is a runtime error, because they can detect you forgot to resolve it first. That's why so many Q# snippets end with a measurement right before the block's scope ends. Contrast this with Qiskit, where qubits are indices into a circuit object built first and run later — Q#'s use statement means allocation is dynamic, happening as the program actually runs, interleaved with ordinary classical control flow.
Next lesson takes the operation-versus-function split further: why functions are forbidden from touching qubits at all, and what that compiler-enforced boundary actually buys you.
